### page_1
Geophys. J. R. astr. Soc. (1980) 62,133-153 
Palaeomagnetic and K-Ar age studies of a 6 km-thick 
Cretaceous section from the Chilean Andes 
H. c. Palmer and A. Hayatsu Department of Geophysics, 
The University of Western Ontario, London, Ontario, Canada N6A 5B7 
W. D. MacDonald Department of Geological sciences, State university 
of New York, Binghampton, New York 13901, USA 
Received 1979 November 1;in original form 1979 May 21 
Summary. Thirty-six palaeomagnetic sampling sites distributed within 
6000m of dominantly andesitic flows and tuffs of Cretaceous age from the 
La Serena area, Chile confirm the normal polarity bias of the Cretaceous 
period. Af, thermal and limited chemical demagnetization techniques have 
been used in testing the stability of the remanent magnetization isolated 
in samples from these sites. A positive fold test in the Quebrada Marquesa 
Formation, the second lowest in the stratigraphic pile, confirms that the 
magnetization isolated is pre-Tertiary in age. Ages calculated by the K-Ar 
whole rock method however, appear to have been variably up-dated probably 
due to argon loss caused by Cretaceous-Tertiary intrusives. Thermal and 
hydrothermal effects of these intrusions have probably reset the magnetiza- 
tion in the youngest formation of the volcanic pile. A composite palaeo- 
magnetic pole calculated from the 30 site poles of the three lower formations 
(209" E, 81" S, &=41/2"), is in good agreement with mid to Late Cretaceous 
poles derived from rock units of the stable platform of South America. The 
use of Andean- Caribbean palaeomagnetic data however, to resolve small 
time-dependent polar shifts within the Cretaceous and thus to estimate the 
time of opening of the south Atlantic is questioned. Many of the Andean- 
Caribbean Cretaceous poles appear to have been affected by local tectonic 
rotation. 
Geology of the Cretaceous units 
The rocks immediately to the east of La Serena, north central Chile, provide an opportunity 
to study the palaeomagnetic history of a substantial portion of Cretaceous time for the 
Andean region of South America. The stratigraphy and structure of this region has been 
worked out in considerable detail by Aguirre & Egert (1965, 1970). The geological summary 
which follows is drawn from their studies, and supplemented by our own petrographic 
studies.

Figure 1. Geological map of the Quebrada Marquesa Quadrangle and the eastern part of the Lambert 
Quadrangle simplified from the maps of Aguhe & Egert (1965, 1970). The location of this area is 
indicated as site 12 on Fig. 7@). 
A simplified geological map (Fig. 1) shows about 6000 m of Cretaceous section, divided 
into four formations. The lower three formations have been further sub-divided into 
additional members. All four formations are composed primarily of lavas, tuff-breccias and 
tuffs of andesitic composition and volcaniclastic sandstones and shales. The units which we 
sampled are from the stratigraphically lowest to highest: the Arqueros Formation, the 
Quebrada Marquesa Formation, the VGita Formation, and the Elquinos Formation. 
The Arqueros Formation consists of three primarily volcanic members dominated by 
feldspar-phyric andesites separated by two primarily sedimentary members containing a 
shallow water marine fauna. That fauna places the formation in the Hauterivian-Barremian 
stages of the Early Cretaceous. Our sampling sites in this formation are in members 1,3 and 
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/62/1/133/620108 by Curtin University Library user on 29 April 2026

### page_3
Palaeomagnetism and K-Ar age studies of the Chilean Andes 135 
5 of Aguirre & Egert (1965). The base of the Arqueros Formation is not exposed, and there- 
fore the foundation on which this volcanic pile rests is not known. 
The Quebrada Marquesa Formation rests conformably on the Arqueros Formation and 
has been divided into four members. The lower three members contain a high proportion of 
tuff-breccias and tuffs of andesitic composition. Most of these volcanic products have under- 
gone extensive high-temperature oxidation and the rocks exhibit colour tones in reds and 
purples. The third member in addition contains red coloured sandstones and conglomerates. 
The uppermost member consists dominantly of grey coloured basalt or andesite flows in 
which original phenocrystic olivine now pseudomorphed by earthy haematite gives the rocks 
a distinctive speckled appearance. The lowest member of the Quebrada Marquesa Formation 
contains a few tens of metres of shallow marine limestones and calcareous sandstones 
bearing a number of pelecypod forms which suggest a late Neocomian age for the formation. 
Sedimentary units higher in the formation contain plant remains, exhibit dessication cracks 
and rain-drop imprints and are therefore continental and are entirely lacking in fossils of 
stratigraphic value. 
The overlying Vista Formation, although structurally conformable with the Quebrada 
Marquesa Formation, bears a regional unconformable relationship to the older formation 
(Aguirre & Thomas 1964). The lowest member of the Vista Formation is a conglomerate 
containing clasts derived from units in the Arqueros and Quebrada Marquesa Formations. 
The upper two members, both of which were sampled in the present study, contain grey 
coloured andesitic lavas and tuffs of grey and red colour. The VEta Formation is largely, if 
not entirely non-marine. Poorly preserved indeterminate, fresh-water gastropods are the only 
fossils recovered from this formation; therefore its age is in doubt. Aguirre & Egert (1965) 
place it tentatively in the range late-Albian-early Coniacian. 
The Elquinos Formation, entirely non-marine and also lacking in fossils, is composed of 
lavas and tuffs ranging from basalt to rhyolite. The rhyolite is an ash-flow occurring approxi- 
mately 1400 m above the base of the formation and is exposed outside the limits of Fig. 1. 
All of our sampling sites are between the base of the formation and this distinctive 
ignimbrite unit. The ash-flow has served as a tool in making correlations of the Elquinos 
Formation with other formations of central Chile but these as well are not well defined in 
age. Some authors have suggested that the correlatives of the Elquinos Formation may be as 
young as Early Tertiary. 
The major structure of the area is a broad anticline, broken by numerous high angle faults 
of N-S trend. Because of these faults, the stratigraphically lowest unit, the Arqueros Forma- 
tion, shows only westerly dips. The Quebrada Marquesa, with both east- and west-limb 
exposures in the anticline, allows a fold test. The highest formations, the VGta and 
Elquinos, lie on the east limb and show only homoclinal easterly dips. Both eastward and 
westward of the anticline, the Cretaceous units are invaded by widespread stocks and 
batholiths of diorite and granodiorite. Thus in spite of the great stratigraphic thickness and 
structural variety in this area, a fold test is only possible for the Quebrada Marquesa 
Formation. 
The lavas and tuffs of all four formations are of andesitic composition in which plagio- 
clase is the most abundant mineral both as a phenocryst phase and in the groundmass. In 
none of the rocks examined is the plagioclase completely unaltered; the minerals which 
partially replace the plagioclase are calcite, sericite, chlorite and epidote. The dominant 
ferromagnesian mineral is clinopyroxene. Primary hornblende was noted in only one of the 
40 thin sections examined. Olivine is a minor porphyritic phase in some of the lavas but is 
largely replaced by serpentine-chlorite-haematite assemblages or serpentine-calcite- 
haematite assemblages. The primary ground-mass of most of the rocks examined consists of 
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/62/1/133/620108 by Curtin University Library user on 29 April 2026

### page_4
136 
plagioclase, pyroxene and oxides but the secondary minerals calcite, chlorite and epidote 
are widespread. A complete range in oxidation classes of original titanomagnetite (Wilson & 
Haggerty 1966; Ade-Hall et al. 1968; Haggerty 1976) is present in these rocks with many 
of the grains in the tuffaceous rocks being of the high oxidation classes of 5 and 6. In 
oxidized grains of class 2 and class 3 the 'exolved' ilmenite lamellae are now wholly replaced 
by black sphene, a feature characteristic of burial metamorphism from the base of the 
laumontite zone to the epidote zone (Ade-Hall, Palmer & Hubbard 1971). AU four 
formations have been reheated to conditions of approximately the prehnite-pumpellyite 
facies of metamorphism. This reheating was probably not a burial-type metamorphism 
inasmuch as we noted no correlation of secondary mineral assemblages with stratigraphy. 
Large masses of granodiorite intrude the Cretaceous rocks both to the east and west (Fig. 1). 
Small plugs of intrusive rocks, too small to dustrate on Fig. 1, (see Aguirre & Egert 1965, 
1970) penetrate the volcanic formations of the map area. These volcanic formations may be 
rafted on an underlying granitic mass, in which case secondary minerals result from a diffuse 
contact metamorphism. 
H. C Palmer, A. Hayatsu and W. D. MacDonald 
Palaeomagnetic sampling and laboratory methods 
A collection of 22 block samples (LS series) was made in the map area in 1967 as part of a 
reconnaissance sampling of various Mesozoic units of northern Chile. In 1974 a second 
collection was obtained (QM series) using a portable rock drill in which generally four 
independently oriented cores (samples) were obtained at each of 19 additional sites. The 
azimuthal component of orientation of the field drilled samples was determined with a sun 
compass and checked with a Brunton compass corrected for the local published magnetic 
declination. Agreement of the sun and magnetic bearings to within 3" gives assurance that 
there is no gross orientation problem with the older collection (LS) series which was 
oriented by the magnetic method only. 
In the laboratory, two to four specimens were prepared from each block sample and the 
field-drilled samples were cut into specimens with each core typically yielding two 
specimens. A polished thin section was made from each block sample and from one of the 
samples from each of the QM series sites. Small pairs of chips with a combined mass of about 
0.5 g were prepared from selected samples for use in a Curie balance. 
The early stages of the palaeomagnetic measurements were performed using a PAR 
spinner magnetometer. All measurements of remanence subsequent to the 30mT af de- 
magnetization step and all measurements of NRM following thermal or chemical 
demagnetization treatments were performed with a Schonstedt DSM-1 spinner magneto- 
meter. Alternating field demagnetization was carried out to a maximum of 110 mT (peak) 
using apparatus similar in design to that described by Roy, Reynolds & Sander (1973). TWO 
to four specimens from each block sample and one specimen from each of the 78 QM 
series samples were progressively demagnetized in steps to a routine maximum of 80 mT. 
Minimum dispersion within the range of a defined stable end-point was used as the criterion 
for selection of the cleaned direction to represent each site. Step-wise thermal demagnetiza- 
tion was carried out on selected samples and sites. In some experiments the thermal de- 
magnetization was performed on specimens which had previously been subjected to the 
partial alternating field treatment ; in other experiments the thermal demagnetization was 
done on specimens which had not been so treated. The thermal demagnetization was done in 
furnaces employing nested mumetal shielding. One of the demagnetizers is a Schonstedt 
TSD-1 model; the other is a hand-crafted unit in which the specimens can be slowly rotated 
dong one axis during the cooling cycle. This rotation minimizes the possible acquisition of

Paheornagnetism and K-Ar age studies of the Chilean Andes 141 
small PTRM’s in one plane due to incomplete dc field cancellation. Temperature calibration 
experiments, temperature gradient measurements and duplicate runs in this furnace and in 
the TSD-I indicate that temperatures (Tables 1-4 and subsequent figures) are conservatively 
estimated to be accurate to k 5°C. Chemical demagnetization involving successive 
immersions in 10N HC1, was performed on specimens of two samples of red sandstones 
from the Quebrada Marquesa Formation. Preferential destruction of the red pigment, ahead 
in time of the larger detrital haematite grains, was aided by specimen serration with a small 
thin-walled drill in the manner described and illustrated by Morris & Carmichael (1978). 
Jst versus T curves were obtained by heating and cooling small chips in air in a constant 
gradient field by a null method in a horizontal translation balance; at the null position the 
applied field used was 0.8 T. 
Palaeomagnetic results 
For this collection 77 per cent of the samples have median destructive af fields of NRM 
in excess of 30 mT and 33 per cent of the total have MDF’s in excess of 80 mT. In general, 
af demagnetization serves to increase the precision of each formational mean direction but 
without producing large directional changes in any individual sample or site mean i.e. the 
directions are well grouped initially. 
The samples from three field-drilled sites in the Quebrada Marquesa Formation (QM 7, 
9 and 11) and the specimens from one block sample from the Arqueros Formation (LS-19) 
proved to be either magnetically unstable or showed poor within-site directional agreement 
throughout the af demagnetization treatment. These samples and sites are rejected from all 
subsequent analysis. 
The palaeomagnetic directional results are given in Tables 1-4 and are graphically 
displayed in Fig. 2. In the statistical tables where two or more entries appear for a sample or 
site corresponding to results obtained by af, thermal or chemical treatment, the entry having 
a calculated pole is the result used in the graphical display of Fig. 2. 
With respect to Fig. 2 and Tables 1-4, the following observatims can be made: 
(1) All samples and sites, with the exception of LS-12 which is the stratigraphically 
youngest sample in the youngest formation, are of normal polarity. 
(2) Although the NRM results from the Arqueros Formation are better grouped than are 
the ‘cleaned’ directions, the NRM results are degraded by the application of the structural 
tilt correction whereas the ‘cleaned’ directions are slightly better grouped when the bedding 
correction is applied. 
(3) Application of the structural tilt correction to the ‘cleaned’ Quebrada Marquesa data 
increases the precision of the mean direction significantly (significant at the 95 per cent 
confidence level, McElhinny 1964). This indicates that a Cretaceous magnetization has been 
isolated. The precision of the mean from the Arqueros and Vista Formations is also 
increased upon application of the structural correction but not significantly. A significant 
improvement is not to be expected however, as the latter formations have homoclinal dips. 
(4) Application of the structural tilt correction to the sites within the youngest 
formation, the Elquinos Formation, results in a degradation of the precision of the mean 
direction. This is probably the result of several of the sites having been remagnetized by 
post-Elquinos intrusions which are particularly abundant in the eastern part of the area of 
study . 
It has been established for some time that the reversal frequency during the Cretaceous 
period differed markedly from that of the Tertiary and that Cretaceous time was dominated 
by fields of normal polarity (Sasajima & Shimada 1966; Helsley & Steiner 1969). A 25 Myr

formations studied. In the middle column are shown the Same sample/site directions after af or thermal 
demagnetization. In the third column these cleaned directions are shown with the structural tik 
correction applied. A fold test, with positive results, was only possible for the Quebrada Marques 
Formation. North-seeking directions are plotted as X's (dots) on the upper (lower) hemisphere. The solid 
triangle is the present Earth's field direction at La Serena. 
uninterrupted normal polarity zone extends from the Aptian to the Coniacian stages of 
the Cretaceous as inferred from seafloor magnetic anomaly patterns (Larson & Pitman 
1972). This time period of normal polarity is compatible with the known age of the 
Quebrada Marquesa and Vizita Formations. However, one might possibly expect to find 
some reversely magnetized sites in the Arqueros Formation if its age assignment to the 
Neocomian is correct. All of our samples from the Arqueros Formation are of normal

Palaeomugnetism and K-Ar age studies of the Chilean Andes 143 
polarity which may indicate that the magnetizations which we have isolated are primary and 
vere acquired in normal polarity fields during this time of normal polarity bias (Irving & 
aoIlaiah 1976) or that some or all of them were originally reversely magnetized but have 
subsequently been remagnetized in later Cretaceous normal polarity fields. Therefore 
&ailed progressive thermal demagnetization was performed on a substantial part of the 
dection in an effort to uncover any reversely magnetized components which might be 
hidden in the total NRM. Progressive chemical leaching experiments were also performed on 
several suitable red sandstones for the same purpose. A few typical results of these experi- 
ments are given below. 
In Fig. 3 are shown the results from af and thermal demagnetization on two specimens 
from the Quebrada Marquesa sample LS- 1. In terms of remanence coercivity LS 1-1 is very 
rypical of much of the collection with only small directional changes experienced during 
removal of the low coercivity components; substantial remanence exceeds the 80 mT limit 
of the experiment but the thermal treatment (LS 1-4) reveals no other distinct directional 
components which can be separated on the basis of blocking temperatures. 
In Fig. 4 are shown the results of sequential af and thermal demagnetization on specimens 
from the Arqueros and Quebrada Marquesa Formations. Judging from the low values of 
saturation magnetization and the hard coercivity of NRM, haematite is the sole magnetic 
phase in these rocks. Both exhibit square shouldered unblocking curves with no evidence of 
anything more than a single component of remanence. 
Chemical demagnetization could be performed on only a small fraction of the collection 
as not much emphasis was placed on the sampling of interbedded sedimentary rocks. 
Member 3 of the Quebrada Marquesa Formation is composed almost entirely of sedimentary 
units, however, and two samples of red sandstones were collected from it. Specimens of 
these samples, LS-15 and LS-16, were subjected to repeated immersions in 10N HC1 
followed by washing and drying in field-free space. Because these rocks contain calcite, as a 
cement and as a replacement of detrital grains, destruction of the red pigment throughout

~e specimens was relatively rapid. The results from the chemical leaching of two serrated

remained high up to the total of 164 hr immersion, followed by greater within-specimen

significance should be attached to the slight directional shifts in both samples following 
rhe 340 hr treatment. In general the limited chemical demagnetization work confirms the

(Fig. 5 and Table 2).

### page_15
Palaeomagnetism and K-Ar age studies of the Chilean Andes 147 
without directional change over the 300-400°C interval. This suggests that an antiparallel 
component is being removed over this temperature range. The lower part of Fig. 6 shows the 
results obtained from two specimens of LS-5 one of which was examined by the af method 
and the other by the thermal demagnetization technique. The af method effects no 
directional or intensity change in LS-5-1. Although LS-5-3 undergoes no significant 
directional changes until it is effectively unblocked at the 670 and 675°C runs, there is a 
pronounced intensity rise in the 600-650°C interval. This might suggest again, as with 
LS-21-4, removal of an antiparallel component, i.e. a reversed component over this tempera- 
ture range. However, there is another plausible explanation. The .Isat versus T curve (inset of 
Fig. 6) exhibits a pronounced increase in saturation magnetization upon cooling from high 
-aperatwe. This indicates that the heating process itself results in the production of a 
mongly magnetic phase which is not present prior to the heating. Thus the evidence of 
reversed components is meagre. The simplest interpretation of all the data is that the 
characteristic normal magnetizations are primary but in a few samples these normal 
magnetizations may have been overprinted by a small secondary reversed component. It is 
aiS0 of course possible that the characteristic normal magnetizations are secondary and that 
only in a few samples has the characteristic primary reversed magnetization survived. In 
&her case, however, the secondary component is antiparallel to the primary component and 
zherefore the age difference between them is likely to be small; the axis of magnetization is 
xhus likely to be a Cretaceous one. 
K-Ar dating 
Thin section examination was used in the initial selection of samples for K-Ar analysis. 
So samples could be found in the collection which were completely free of secondary 
mineral alteration. In fact, all our samples from the Arqueros formation have such a heavy 
&cite overprint on the plagioclase that no representatives from this formation were 
selected for analysis. Initially only three samples were selected, one from each of the three 
vounger formations. The calculated ages from these three samples were all younger than

### page_16
148 H. C Palmer, A. Hayatsu and W. D. MacDonald 
expected. Accordingly, additional samples were selected from a single formation, the 
Quebrada Marquesa Formation, to test whether argon loss or the presence of initial argon 
was an important factor in these samples. 
All samples studied were crushed to pass 20 mesh with powders finer than 100 mesh 
being discarded. Each sample was then split into two portions, one of which was further 
crushed to pass 100 mesh and used for potassium analysis. The other portion was loaded 
into an argon extraction system immediately after crushing, and baked for 18 hr at 190"C, 
followed by an argon extraction. 
The results are given in Table 5. The older apparent ages appear in the oldest formation, 
the Quebrada Marquesa. However, younger ages equal to those in the younger VGita and 
Elquinos Formations are present in samples from the Quebrada Marquesa Formation. 
Because a significant unconformity is present between the Quebrada Marquesa and the 
VGta Formation and because the apparent ages within the Quebrada Marquesa Formation 
are not stratigraphically ordered, none of the ages given in Table 5 is considered to give a 
valid estimate of the time of formation. An isochron plot of the Quebrada Marquesa data 
shows considerable scatter of the data points with no evidence that the samples share a 
common 'initial' argon component. The discordance is most readily explained by variable 
argon loss subsequent to deposition. 
Discussion 
Individual formation poles are given in Tables 1-4. Because the data from the Elquinos 
Formation are degraded by the application of the structural tilt corrections, it is inferred 
that some or all of the sites within this formation have acquired post-Elquinos magnetiza- 
tions. The data from this formation are rejected. 
The Quebrada Marquesa pole (Table 2) and the VGita Formation pole (Table 3) are 
different at the 95 per cent confidence limit. This may reflect polar wander, incomplete 
averaging of secular variation or some combination of secondary overprints and local 
tectonic complexities. Inasmuch as these possible causes cannot be resolved, a composite 
Cretaceous palaeomagnetic pole is calculated (209" E, 8 1" S, Ag5 = 4%") by averaging the 
30 valid site poles from the Arqueros, Quebrada Marquesa and ViEita formations. This pole 
is very close to the composite pole (220" E, 85" S, Ag5 = 6") recently reported by Valencio 
et al. (1977) for the time interval: late Early Cretaceous-Late Cretaceous. However, the 
stratigraphic age of the Arqueros Formation (Hauterivian-Barremian) is included in their 
definition of their early Early Cretaceous 'age group' of poles. The Arqueros pole does not 
fall in this 'age group' but is indistinguishable from those placed in the younger 'time group' 
- late Early Cretaceous to Late Cretaceous. Two explanations can be offered: remagnetiza- 
tion and tectonic rotation, as described below. 
Late Cretaceous remagnetization of the Arqueros Formation 
In spite of careful laboratory work directed at uncovering secondary components in the La 
Serena area rocks, this possibility of remagnetization of the Arqueros Formation in a later 
Cretaceous normal polarity field, still exists. The distinctive porphyritic andesites of the 
Arqueros Formation contributed clasts to the lowest conglomerate-rich member of the 
VGita Formation. Therefore future palaeomagnetic work in this area could profitably be 
directed to performing a conglomerate test using these distinctive clasts. This test would 
establish whether or not the andesites of the Arqueros Formation have retained a pre-late 
Cretaceous magnetization. 
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/62/1/133/620108 by Curtin University Library user on 29 April 2026

Local tectonic rotation in orogenic belts 
In Table 6 we tabulate South American Cretaceous palaeomagnetic poles. Rather than sub- 
dividing this list on the basis of age within the Cretaceous period we have grouped the poles 
on the basis of tectonic setting of site locations: A, sites overlying the Precambrian stable 
platform and B, sites from the Andean-Caribbean fold belts. These sites, together with their 
corresponding poles are graphically displayed in Fig. 7(a) and (b). Although some sites from 
the orogenic belt yield poles in agreement with those from the stable platform, many are 
discordant and a few are very discordant. We interpret this to mean that sites within fold 
Figure 7. Cretaceous sites and their corresponding poles numbered as in Table 6, (a) displays poles from

belt. Pole 12 is that derived from this study. The poles from the orogenic regions are more widely 
dispersed than those from the stable platform.

### page_20
152 
belts are subject to tectonic rotations - rotations which are not always evident with the 
tools of classical structural geology. Thus the use of palaeomagnetic data from orogenic 
belts to detect or confirm time-dependent polar shifts is likely to be hazardous. 
In conclusion, we attribute the dispersion of Cretaceous poles for sites in the orogenic 
zones to local tectonic rotations. On the basis of evidence presently available from the 
tectonically stable platform of South America, no clear pattern of polar shift during the 
Cretaceous is perceptible. The best estimate of the mean Cretaceous pole for South America 
(mean of poles of Fig. 7a) is 85'S, 0.52' E, Ag5=41/io. Relative to that pole, the Serena 
Cretaceous volcanic section of central Chile appears to have undergone only a minor 
clockwise rotation, of approximately 15' f 11'. 
H C Palmer, A. Hayatsu and W. D. MacDonald
